notes.front: In SSB, what is the upper sideband (USB)?
notes.back: The sideband on the higher-frequency side of the carrier. SSB transmits only one sideband: upper (USB) or lower (LSB).
notes.explanation: Either sideband carries the whole message, but only if the transmitter and receiver are set to the same one, so amateurs follow a convention for each band.
notes.example: For SSB on 10 m, VHF and UHF, amateurs normally use upper sideband.
notes.source: US Army, FM 24-18, Tactical Single-Channel Radio Communications Techniques (1987), para 2-6 (“Single Sideband”); NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8A06

notes.front: What is WSJT-X, in one sentence?
notes.back: A computer program for weak-signal radio contacts between amateurs; FT8 is one of its digital modes.
notes.explanation: Its signal processing makes contacts over unusual paths practical, such as signals bounced off the trails of meteors (meteor scatter) or off the Moon (moonbounce).
notes.example: WSJT-X supports Earth-Moon-Earth (moonbounce) contacts, in which signals are reflected off the Moon.
notes.source: Wikipedia, “WSJT (amateur radio software)”; NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8D10

notes.front: What is packet radio, in one sentence?
notes.back: Digital radio that sends data in packets, each with a header that carries call signs.
notes.explanation: In the usual amateur packet protocol every packet carries the sender’s call sign, so the station identifies itself by data emission, which the FCC rules allow; any packet station can also act as a digipeater that relays others.
notes.example: APRS position reports are sent as packets and relayed by digipeaters; VHF packet usually uses FM or PM.
notes.source: Wikipedia, “Packet radio”; NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8A02, T8D08; 47 CFR 97.119(b)(3)

notes.front: What is APRS, in one sentence?
notes.back: Automatic Packet Reporting System: real-time digital reporting of local information, such as GPS positions, shown on a map.
notes.explanation: It carries data like GPS coordinates, weather-station telemetry and text messages on a shared frequency, relayed by digipeaters and the internet.
notes.example: During a public-service event, APRS shows each checkpoint's and vehicle's position on a live map at net control.
notes.source: Wikipedia, “Automatic Packet Reporting System”; NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8D05

notes.front: What does PSK stand for, and what does it change?
notes.back: Phase Shift Keying: a digital mode that carries data by shifting the phase of the carrier.
notes.explanation: Phase is where the wave is in its cycle. PSK is the phase counterpart of on-off CW keying: in the simple two-state form, a one reverses the phase (a 180-degree shift) and a zero leaves it unchanged.
notes.example: The bits 1, 0, 1 go out as a phase reversal, no change, then another reversal.
notes.source: US Navy, NEETS Module 12 (NAVEDTRA 14184), Modulation, chapter 2, “Phase-Shift Keying”; NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8D06

notes.front: What is NTSC, in one sentence?
notes.back: An analog fast-scan colour TV signal.
notes.explanation: Slow-scan TV, by contrast, sends still pictures. Amateur fast-scan TV sent with AM needs about 6 MHz of bandwidth, far wider than any voice mode.
notes.example: Contrast: an SSB voice signal is about 3 kHz wide, so one AM fast-scan TV signal takes the room of about 2,000 of them.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8D04, T8A10, T8A08; Wikipedia, “Slow-scan television”

notes.front: What is ARQ, in one sentence?
notes.back: Automatic repeat request: an error-correction method in which the receiving station detects errors and asks for retransmission.
notes.explanation: The receiver acknowledges good data; if the sender gets no acknowledgement in time, it sends the data again.
notes.example: Like a listener saying “say again” whenever part of a message is garbled, but done automatically by the software.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8D11; Wikipedia, “Automatic repeat request”

notes.front: What is an amateur radio mesh network, in one sentence?
notes.back: An amateur-radio data network using commercial Wi-Fi equipment with modified firmware.
notes.explanation: Nodes connect richly to one another, so data can take several routes. Broadband-Hamnet, for example, focuses on emergency communication.
notes.example: Broadband-Hamnet is an amateur mesh-networking project on 2.4 GHz: a self-configuring, fault-tolerant wireless computer network.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8D12; Wikipedia, “Wireless mesh network”

notes.front: What is an amateur radio satellite, in one sentence?
notes.back: A space station on an earth satellite, used for the same purposes as the amateur service: it relays signals between amateur stations.
notes.explanation: Different satellites act as repeaters, as linear transponders (which relay signals live, as they arrive) or as store-and-forward relays (which hold messages and send them later), carrying voice (FM, SSB) and data.
notes.example: Many carry an OSCAR designation (Orbiting Satellite Carrying Amateur Radio), assigned by AMSAT.
notes.source: 47 CFR 2.1 (“Amateur-Satellite Service”); Wikipedia, “Amateur radio satellite”

notes.front: In satellite work, what is the uplink?
notes.back: The frequency or band you transmit on to reach the satellite.
notes.explanation: Your signal goes up on the uplink and the satellite sends it back down on another frequency, the downlink (next card). Anyone allowed to transmit on the uplink frequency may be the control operator of a station using the satellite.
notes.example: A satellite with a 70 cm uplink hears stations transmitting in the 70 cm band.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T1E02, T8B12; Wikipedia, “Amateur radio satellite”

notes.front: In satellite work, what is the downlink?
notes.back: The frequency or band on which the satellite transmits back to Earth; you listen there.
notes.explanation: Satellite modes are named uplink band first, then downlink band, so you know where to transmit and where to listen.
notes.example: A satellite with a 2 m downlink is heard by tuning a receiver to the 2 m band.
notes.source: Wikipedia, “Amateur radio satellite”; NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8B12

notes.front: What is a linear transponder on an amateur satellite?
notes.back: The satellite’s relay for two-way contacts in real time; since 1965 most OSCAR satellites have carried one.
notes.explanation: It retransmits what it hears on the uplink onto the downlink as it happens, unlike a store-and-forward relay that holds messages for later.
notes.example: An SSB contact through a linear transponder happens live, like talking through a repeater in the sky.
notes.source: Wikipedia, “Amateur radio satellite”; NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8B12

notes.front: In the FCC rules, what is telemetry?
notes.back: A one-way transmission of measurements made at a distance from the measuring instrument.
notes.explanation: Space telemetry is the same from a space station: measurements made in the spacecraft, including how it is functioning.
notes.example: A satellite sending down its health and status, so people on the ground can see how it is working.
notes.source: 47 CFR 97.3(a)(46), (a)(42); NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8B01
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US government work, 17 USC 105)

notes.front: What is a satellite beacon?
notes.back: A transmission from a satellite that contains status information.
notes.explanation: Its telemetry reports the satellite's health and status, and its steady signal is a reference for how strong the downlink is.
notes.example: Contrast: a beacon station on Earth transmits so others can observe propagation; a satellite beacon reports on the satellite.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8B05, T8B01, T8B12

notes.front: What is Doppler shift in satellite communications?
notes.back: An observed change in signal frequency caused by relative motion between the satellite and the Earth station.
notes.explanation: A satellite approaching you is heard higher in frequency, and lower as it moves away, so you retune during a pass.
notes.example: The same effect as a passing vehicle's pitch: higher as it approaches, lower as it recedes.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8B07; Wikipedia, “Doppler effect”

notes.front: What is a satellite tracking program?
notes.back: Software that shows where a satellite is and predicts its passes over your station.
notes.explanation: It gives the time, the azimuth (direction round the horizon) and the elevation (angle above the horizon) of the start, highest point and end of a pass, plus a real-time map and the Doppler-shifted frequency.
notes.example: Before a pass, the program tells you the satellite rises in the south-west at a given minute and how high it will climb.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8B03; Wikipedia, “Horizontal coordinate system”

notes.front: What are Keplerian elements?
notes.back: The set of parameters that uniquely identifies a satellite's orbit; tracking programs take them as input.
notes.explanation: A real orbit changes over time, so the elements are updated and the program must be given current ones.
notes.example: Like a recipe for the orbit: with a current set, the software can work out where the satellite will be.
notes.source: Wikipedia, “Orbital elements”; NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8B06

notes.front: What does LEO mean for a communication satellite?
notes.back: Low Earth Orbit, which has a period of around 100 minutes.
notes.explanation: Most artificial objects in space are in LEO, which is usually defined as an orbital period of 128 minutes or less.
notes.example: At about 100 minutes per orbit, a LEO satellite circles the Earth roughly 14 times a day.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8B10; Wikipedia, “Low Earth orbit”

notes.front: What is spin fading of satellite signals?
notes.back: Fading caused by rotation of the satellite and its antennas.
notes.explanation: As the satellite and its antennas rotate, the received signal strength rises and falls.
notes.example: Like a lighthouse beam that seems to pulse because the lamp is turning, not because it is dimming.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8B09

notes.front: What does it mean if a satellite is in U/V mode?
notes.back: Its uplink is in the 70 cm band and its downlink in the 2 m band.
notes.explanation: Satellite modes name the uplink band first and the downlink band second; U is the UHF band, V the VHF band.
notes.example: In U/V mode you transmit on about 435 MHz and listen on about 145 MHz.

image.alt: Diagram: a ground station sends its uplink to the satellite on the 70 cm band (UHF, 420–450 MHz); the satellite sends its downlink back to Earth on the 2 m band (VHF, 144–148 MHz).
image.credit: Drawn for this deck from NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8B08, and 47 CFR 97.301(a)

notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8B08; 47 CFR 97.207(c)(2) (space-station segments 144–146 and 435–438 MHz); Wikipedia, “Amateur radio satellite”

notes.front: What is radio direction finding, in one sentence?
notes.back: Locating a transmitter by working out the direction its signal comes from, usually with a directional antenna.
notes.explanation: It is how amateurs track down sources of noise interference or jamming, and the basis of hidden-transmitter hunts.
notes.example: In a “fox hunt”, competitors carry a receiver and a directional antenna and race to find hidden transmitters.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8C01, T8C02; Wikipedia, “Amateur radio direction finding”

notes.front: What is contesting, in amateur radio?
notes.back: A competition to contact as many stations as possible during a set period, exchanging specified information.
notes.explanation: Each contest's rules set the bands, the modes and the exchange; contacts earn points, and results are published.
notes.example: In a contest weekend, a station might exchange just a call sign, signal report and location with hundreds of others.
notes.source: Wikipedia, “Contesting”; NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8C03

notes.front: What is a grid locator?
notes.back: A letter-number designator assigned to a geographic location.
notes.explanation: Grid locators (Maidenhead locators, grid squares) describe a station's position concisely and survive noisy conditions.
notes.example: A locator such as KN28LH names a small area of the Earth; digital modes like FT8 exchange them in every contact.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8C05; Wikipedia, “Maidenhead Locator System”

notes.front: What is Voice Over Internet Protocol (VoIP)?
notes.back: A method of delivering voice communications over the internet using digital techniques.
notes.explanation: Amateur linking systems, introduced in the next cards, use it to carry voice between distant stations and repeaters.
notes.example: A local repeater in Ohio can be linked over the internet to one in Australia, so handheld users talk across the world.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8C07, T8C08; Wikipedia, “EchoLink”

notes.front: What is the Internet Radio Linking Project (IRLP)?
notes.back: A technique to connect amateur radio systems, such as repeaters, via the internet.
notes.explanation: Each IRLP node is a computer connected to a radio and the internet; users always talk from a radio and use DTMF tones to connect nodes.
notes.example: A handheld user keys a node number with DTMF tones, and the local repeater links to a distant IRLP node.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8C08; Wikipedia, “Internet Radio Linking Project”

notes.front: What is EchoLink, in one sentence?
notes.back: A computer-based system that links amateurs by VoIP over the internet, including through radio stations and repeaters.
notes.explanation: A user can connect from a computer without a radio, but must first register a call sign and provide proof of licence.
notes.example: An amateur travelling abroad uses EchoLink on a laptop to talk through the home repeater.
notes.source: Wikipedia, “EchoLink”; NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8C09, T8C10

notes.front: What is a gateway, in amateur linking?
notes.back: An amateur radio station that connects other amateur stations to the internet.
notes.explanation: It is the bridge between on-air users and an internet linking system; an IRLP node, for example, joins a radio to the internet.
notes.example: A club station with a radio and an internet connection lets local handheld users reach an internet linking network.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8C11; Wikipedia, “Internet Radio Linking Project”

notes.front: Under the FCC's emission classes, single sideband (SSB) is a form of {{c1::amplitude modulation}}.
notes.explanation: 47 CFR 2.201 lists single-sideband emissions (full, reduced or suppressed carrier) under carriers that are amplitude-modulated.
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US government work, 17 USC 105)

notes.front: In the FCC's emission classes, how are FM and PM related?
notes.back: Both are angle modulation; wherever FM is indicated, PM is also acceptable.
notes.explanation: That is why the pool's answers say “FM or PM” for repeaters and VHF packet.
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US government work, 17 USC 105)

notes.front: For SSB on 10 m, VHF and UHF, amateurs normally use the {{c1::upper}} sideband.
notes.explanation: USB is the convention on 10 m and above; both stations must use the same sideband to hear each other properly.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8A06

notes.front: A CW signal needs about {{c1::150 Hz}} of bandwidth, the narrowest of the common modes.
notes.explanation: CW is just a carrier switched on and off, so it needs far less room than any voice mode.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8A11, T8A05

notes.front: A typical SSB voice signal is about {{c1::3 kHz}} wide.
notes.explanation: That is why the best receive filter for SSB is about 2400 Hz: wide enough for speech, no wider.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8A08, T4B10

notes.front: An FM voice signal on a VHF repeater is between {{c1::10 and 15 kHz}} wide.
notes.explanation: FM needs several times the bandwidth of SSB, which is about 3 kHz wide.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8A09, T8A08

notes.front: AM fast-scan TV needs about {{c1::6 MHz}} of bandwidth.
notes.explanation: Moving colour pictures carry far more information than a voice, so they need thousands of times the bandwidth.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8A10

notes.front: What is a disadvantage of FM compared with SSB when two stations transmit on the same frequency?
notes.back: An FM receiver receives only one signal at a time.
notes.explanation: With two FM signals on one frequency, you hear only one of them, not both together.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8A12

notes.front: What three things do packet radio transmissions include?
notes.back: A checksum for error detection, a header with the destination's call sign, and automatic repeat request (ARQ) on error.
notes.explanation: These let packet stations address messages, spot corrupted data and have it sent again automatically.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8D08

notes.front: What three kinds of data does the pool say APRS can transmit?
notes.back: GPS position data, text messages and weather data.
notes.explanation: APRS carries any information of immediate local value; positions are its best-known use, shown on a live map.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8D03, T8D05; Wikipedia, “Automatic Packet Reporting System”

notes.front: Which three operating activities do the digital modes in WSJT-X support?
notes.back: Earth-Moon-Earth (moonbounce), weak-signal propagation beacons and meteor scatter.
notes.explanation: Moonbounce signals travel to the Moon and back; meteor scatter uses brief reflections from the trails of meteors; propagation beacons transmit so others can observe propagation. All involve very weak or very brief signals, which is what WSJT-X’s modes are designed to decode.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8D10; Wikipedia, “WSJT (amateur radio software)”; 47 CFR 97.3(a)(9)

notes.front: Which transmission modes do amateur radio satellites commonly use?
notes.back: All of SSB, FM and CW/data.
notes.explanation: Different satellites carry FM repeaters, SSB/CW linear transponders or digital relays.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8B04; Wikipedia, “Amateur radio satellite”

notes.front: Satellite beacons typically transmit telemetry on the satellite's {{c1::health and status}}.
notes.explanation: Telemetry means measurements sent from a distance; for a satellite, that is how its systems are working.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8B01, T8B05

notes.front: Who is permitted to receive telemetry from an amateur radio satellite?
notes.back: Anyone.
notes.explanation: No licence or permission is needed just to receive it, even though the rules let space telemetry be sent as specially coded messages.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8B11; 47 CFR 97.207(f)

notes.front: Using excessive effective radiated power on a satellite uplink {{c1::blocks access by other users}}.
notes.explanation: Effective radiated power is the power fed to the antenna multiplied by the antenna’s gain. Everyone shares the satellite, and an overly strong uplink signal crowds other users out.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8B02; 47 CFR 2.1 (“Effective Radiated Power”)

notes.front: How can you tell your uplink power into a linear transponder satellite is neither too low nor too high?
notes.back: Your signal on the downlink should be about as strong as the satellite's beacon.
notes.explanation: The beacon is a steady reference; matching it means you are loud enough without taking more than your share.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8B12

notes.front: What three things does a satellite tracking program provide?
notes.back: A real-time map of the satellite's track; time, azimuth and elevation of each pass; and the Doppler-shifted frequency.
notes.explanation: Together these tell you when to listen, where to point and what frequency to tune.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8B03

notes.front: The data a satellite tracking program needs as input are the satellite's {{c1::Keplerian elements}}.
notes.explanation: The elements define the orbit, so from them the program computes where and when the satellite will appear.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8B06

notes.front: For a hidden transmitter hunt, the most useful item is a {{c1::directional antenna}}.
notes.explanation: Radio direction finding depends on finding the bearing of strongest signal, which a directional antenna shows.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8C02

notes.front: When contacting a station in a contest, what should you send?
notes.back: Only the minimum information needed for proper identification and the contest exchange.
notes.explanation: Short exchanges keep the frequency moving; full call signs are still required for identification.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8C04

notes.front: What is required before you can use EchoLink?
notes.back: Register your call sign and provide proof of licence.
notes.explanation: Because EchoLink can reach radios without using one, it checks that each user is licensed.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8C10

notes.front: How does a user with a radio connect a local IRLP node to another node?
notes.back: By sending DTMF tones from the radio.
notes.explanation: Each node has a number; the user keys it in with DTMF, and IRLP users always talk from a radio, never a computer.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8C06; Wikipedia, “Internet Radio Linking Project”

notes.front: Which of the following is a form of amplitude modulation?
notes.back: Single sideband
notes.choices:
A) Spread spectrum
B) Packet radio
C) Single sideband
D) Phase shift keying (PSK)
notes.choicesExplained: A: spread spectrum spreads a signal across a wide band; it is not a form of AM. B: packet radio is a digital data system, not a modulation type. D: PSK changes phase, not amplitude.
notes.explanation: SSB is amplitude modulation with one sideband (and usually the carrier) removed.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8A01

notes.front: What type of modulation is commonly used for VHF packet radio transmissions?
notes.back: FM or PM
notes.choices:
A) FM or PM
B) SSB
C) AM
D) PSK
notes.choicesExplained: B: SSB is the weak-signal voice mode, not the usual VHF packet modulation. C: AM is not the usual packet modulation. D: PSK is a digital keying method, not the usual VHF packet modulation.
notes.explanation: VHF packet radio is commonly sent with FM or PM, the same modulation used on VHF repeaters.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8A02

notes.front: Which type of voice mode is often used for long-distance (weak signal) contacts on the VHF and UHF bands?
notes.back: SSB
notes.choices:
A) FM
B) DRM
C) SSB
D) PM
notes.choicesExplained: A and D: FM and PM are used for local repeater and simplex work, not weak-signal work. B: DRM (Digital Radio Mondiale) is not the usual amateur weak-signal voice mode.
notes.explanation: SSB drops the carrier and one sideband, so all the power goes into one narrow voice signal (about 3 kHz); the US Army uses it for greater reliability and long range without loss of intelligibility from fading. That suits weak-signal VHF and UHF contacts.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8A03, T8A08; US Army, FM 24-18, Tactical Single-Channel Radio Communications Techniques (1987), para 2-6

notes.front: Which type of modulation is commonly used for VHF and UHF voice repeaters?
notes.back: FM or PM
notes.choices:
A) AM
B) SSB
C) PSK
D) FM or PM
notes.choicesExplained: A: AM is not used on typical voice repeaters. B: SSB is for weak-signal work, not repeaters. C: PSK is a digital data mode, not a voice repeater mode.
notes.explanation: FM is the usual voice mode on VHF and higher bands, and the FCC accepts phase modulation wherever FM is indicated; that is why the pool keys “FM or PM”.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8A04; US Army, FM 24-18, Tactical Single-Channel Radio Communications Techniques (1987), para 2-5; 47 CFR 2.201(c)(3)

notes.front: Which of the following signal types has the narrowest bandwidth?
notes.back: CW
notes.choices:
A) FM voice
B) SSB voice
C) CW
D) Slow-scan TV
notes.choicesExplained: A: FM voice is 10–15 kHz wide. B: SSB voice is about 3 kHz wide. D: slow-scan TV carries pictures and is wider than CW.
notes.explanation: CW needs only about 150 Hz, far narrower than any of the voice or image modes listed.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8A05

notes.front: Which sideband is normally used for 10-meter HF, VHF, and UHF single-sideband communications?
notes.back: Upper sideband
notes.choices:
A) Upper sideband
B) Lower sideband
C) Suppressed sideband
D) Inverted sideband
notes.choicesExplained: B: either sideband can carry the voice, but both stations must use the same one, and on 10 m, VHF and UHF that is upper sideband. C: the carrier is what is suppressed in SSB, not a sideband. D: SSB is sent on the upper or the lower sideband; there is no “inverted sideband” to choose.
notes.explanation: Both stations must use the same sideband to understand each other, so amateurs keep to upper sideband for SSB on 10 m, VHF and UHF.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8A06; US Army, FM 24-18, Tactical Single-Channel Radio Communications Techniques (1987), para 2-6

notes.front: What is one characteristic of single sideband (SSB) compared to FM?
notes.back: SSB signals have narrower bandwidth
notes.choices:
A) SSB signals are easier to tune in correctly
B) SSB signals are less susceptible to interference
C) SSB signals have narrower bandwidth
D) SSB signals are less susceptible to high SWR
notes.choicesExplained: A: SSB is harder, not easier, to tune in correctly. B: the keyed advantage of SSB is its narrower bandwidth, not lower susceptibility to interference. D: SWR measures how well the antenna and feed line are matched, so it does not depend on the mode.
notes.explanation: SSB occupies about 3 kHz against 10–15 kHz for FM voice.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8A07, T9B12

notes.front: What is the approximate bandwidth of a typical single sideband (SSB) voice signal?
notes.back: 3 kHz
notes.choices:
A) 1 kHz
B) 3 kHz
C) 6 kHz
D) 15 kHz
notes.choicesExplained: A: 1 kHz is too narrow for intelligible speech. C: 6 kHz is twice the width of a typical SSB voice signal. D: 15 kHz is at the top of FM voice width.
notes.explanation: An AM signal carries two sidebands, each as wide as the audio. SSB removes the carrier and one sideband before transmitting, so a voice signal needs only about 3 kHz.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8A08; US Army, FM 24-18, Tactical Single-Channel Radio Communications Techniques (1987), paras 2-5 and 2-6

notes.front: What is the approximate bandwidth of an FM voice signal on VHF repeaters?
notes.back: Between 10 and 15 kHz
notes.choices:
A) Less than 500 Hz
B) About 150 kHz
C) Between 10 and 15 kHz
D) Between 50 and 125 kHz
notes.choicesExplained: A: less than 500 Hz is far too narrow for FM voice; CW needs about 150 Hz. B and D: 50–150 kHz is far wider than amateur FM voice.
notes.explanation: FM carries the voice by swinging the carrier’s frequency to either side of its centre, the louder the further, so it needs several times the width of a 3 kHz SSB signal.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8A09, T8A08; US Army, FM 24-18, Tactical Single-Channel Radio Communications Techniques (1987), para 2-5

notes.front: What is the approximate bandwidth of AM fast-scan TV transmissions?
notes.back: About 6 MHz
notes.choices:
A) More than 10 MHz
B) About 6 MHz
C) About 3 MHz
D) About 1 MHz
notes.choicesExplained: A: more than 10 MHz is too wide. C and D: 1–3 MHz is too narrow for a fast-scan TV signal.
notes.explanation: A fast-scan picture signal needs about 6 MHz, some 2,000 times the width of a 3 kHz SSB voice signal: moving colour pictures carry far more information than a voice.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8A10, T8A08

notes.front: What is the approximate bandwidth required to transmit a CW signal?
notes.back: 150 Hz
notes.choices:
A) 2.4 kHz
B) 150 Hz
C) 1000 Hz
D) 15 kHz
notes.choicesExplained: A: 2.4 kHz is an SSB filter width. C: 1000 Hz is far wider than CW needs. D: 15 kHz is FM voice width.
notes.explanation: A CW signal needs only about 150 Hz.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8A11

notes.front: Which of the following is a disadvantage of FM compared with single sideband?
notes.back: Only one signal can be received at a time
notes.choices:
A) Voice quality is poorer
B) Only one signal can be received at a time
C) FM signals are harder to tune
D) FM signals are more susceptible to high SWR
notes.choicesExplained: A: voice quality is not the keyed weakness of FM. C: it is SSB, not FM, that is harder to tune in correctly. D: SWR does not depend on the modulation type.
notes.explanation: An FM receiver captures the strongest signal, so only one signal can be received at a time.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8A12

notes.front: What telemetry information is typically transmitted by satellite beacons?
notes.back: Health and status of the satellite
notes.choices:
A) The signal strength of received signals
B) Time of day accurate to plus or minus 1/10 second
C) Health and status of the satellite
D) All these choices are correct
notes.choicesExplained: A: received-signal strengths are not typical beacon telemetry. B: precise time of day is not what beacons send. D: since A and B are wrong, “all” is wrong.
notes.explanation: Telemetry is a one-way transmission of measurements from a distance; a satellite beacon sends the satellite’s own measurements, which report its health and status.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8B01, T8B05; 47 CFR 97.3(a)(46)

notes.front: What is the impact of using excessive effective radiated power on a satellite uplink?
notes.back: Blocking access by other users
notes.choices:
A) Possibility of commanding the satellite to an improper mode
B) Blocking access by other users
C) Overloading the satellite batteries
D) Possibility of rebooting the satellite control computer
notes.choicesExplained: A: the uplink carries user signals; power does not command the satellite. C: your signal does not load the satellite's batteries. D: user uplink signals do not reboot the control computer.
notes.explanation: Too much uplink power takes more than your share of the transponder and blocks other users.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8B02

notes.front: Which of the following are provided by satellite tracking programs?
notes.back: All these choices are correct
notes.choices:
A) Maps showing the real-time position of the satellite track over Earth
B) The time, azimuth, and elevation of the start, maximum altitude, and end of a pass
C) The apparent frequency of the satellite transmission, including effects of Doppler shift
D) All these choices are correct
notes.choicesExplained: A, B and C are each only one of the program's outputs; all three are correct.
notes.explanation: Tracking programs give all three: a real-time map of the satellite’s track, the time, azimuth and elevation of each pass, and the frequency you will actually hear once Doppler shift is included.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8B03

notes.front: What mode of transmission is commonly used by amateur radio satellites?
notes.back: All these choices are correct
notes.choices:
A) SSB
B) FM
C) CW/data
D) All these choices are correct
notes.choicesExplained: A, B and C are each only one of the modes in use; all are correct.
notes.explanation: Different satellites carry FM repeaters, SSB and CW linear transponders, or digital relays, so SSB, FM and CW/data are all in common use.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8B04; Wikipedia, “Amateur radio satellite”

notes.front: What is a satellite beacon?
notes.back: A transmission from a satellite that contains status information
notes.choices:
A) The primary transmit antenna on the satellite
B) An indicator light that shows where to point your antenna
C) A reflective surface on the satellite
D) A transmission from a satellite that contains status information
notes.choicesExplained: A: the beacon is a transmission, not the satellite's main antenna. B: it is not a light. C: it is not a reflective surface.
notes.explanation: Its steady signal reports the satellite’s health and status, and on the downlink it also serves as a reference level for setting your own uplink power.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8B05, T8B01, T8B12

notes.front: Which of the following are inputs to a satellite tracking program?
notes.back: The Keplerian elements
notes.choices:
A) The satellite transmitted power
B) The Keplerian elements
C) The last observed time of zero Doppler shift
D) All these choices are correct
notes.choicesExplained: A: transmitted power does not affect where the satellite is. C: the time of zero Doppler is something the program predicts, not what it needs. D: since A and C are wrong, “all” is wrong.
notes.explanation: The Keplerian elements describe the orbit, so the program needs them to predict passes.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8B06

notes.front: What is Doppler shift in reference to satellite communications?
notes.back: An observed change in signal frequency caused by relative motion between the satellite and Earth station
notes.choices:
A) A change in the satellite orbit
B) A mode where the satellite receives signals on one band and transmits on another
C) An observed change in signal frequency caused by relative motion between the satellite and Earth station
D) A special digital communications mode for some satellites
notes.choicesExplained: A: the orbit itself does not change. B: that describes a satellite mode such as U/V. D: it is not a digital mode.
notes.explanation: A satellite coming towards you is heard higher in frequency, and lower as it moves away, so you retune during a pass.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8B07; Wikipedia, “Doppler effect”

notes.front: What does it mean if a satellite is operating in U/V mode?
notes.back: The satellite uplink is in the 70-centimeter band and the downlink is in the 2-meter band
notes.choices:
A) The satellite uplink is in the 15-meter band and the downlink is in the 10-meter band
B) The satellite uplink is in the 70-centimeter band and the downlink is in the 2-meter band
C) The satellite operates using ultraviolet frequencies
D) The satellite frequencies are usually variable
notes.choicesExplained: A: 15 m up and 10 m down is an HF mode, not U/V. C: U and V are radio bands, not ultraviolet. D: the letters name fixed bands, not variable frequencies.
notes.explanation: Mode letters name the uplink band first, then the downlink: U is the UHF band (70 cm), V the VHF band (2 m).

image.alt: Diagram: a ground station sends its uplink to the satellite on the 70 cm band (UHF, 420–450 MHz); the satellite sends its downlink back to Earth on the 2 m band (VHF, 144–148 MHz).
image.credit: Drawn for this deck from NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8B08, and 47 CFR 97.301(a)

notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8B08; Wikipedia, “Amateur radio satellite”

notes.front: What causes spin fading of satellite signals?
notes.back: Rotation of the satellite and its antennas
notes.choices:
A) Circular polarized noise interference radiated from the sun
B) Rotation of the satellite and its antennas
C) Doppler shift of the received signal
D) Interfering signals within the satellite uplink band
notes.choicesExplained: A: solar noise is not the cause. C: Doppler shift changes frequency, not signal strength. D: interfering uplink signals cause interference, not spin fading.
notes.explanation: As the satellite spins, its antennas point toward and then away from you in turn, so the received signal rises and falls.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8B09

notes.front: What does the term LEO mean in reference to communication satellites?
notes.back: Low Earth Orbit, which has a period of around 100 minutes
notes.choices:
A) Low Energy Orbit, which conserves battery power
B) Low Elevation Orbit, which appears close to the horizon from the earth station
C) Low Equilibrium Orbit, which has a slightly unstable period
D) Low Earth Orbit, which has a period of around 100 minutes
notes.choicesExplained: A, B and C: “Energy”, “Elevation” and “Equilibrium” are invented expansions; the E stands for Earth.
notes.explanation: At about 100 minutes per orbit, a LEO satellite circles the Earth about 14 times a day (1,440 minutes ÷ 100).
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8B10

notes.front: Who is permitted to receive telemetry from an amateur radio satellite?
notes.back: Anyone
notes.choices:
A) Anyone
B) Only the satellite control operator
C) Only the control operator or a licensed radio amateur who has received the encryption key from the control operator
D) Only a licensed radio amateur who has received the encryption key from AMSAT
notes.choicesExplained: B: reception is not limited to the control operator. C and D: no encryption key is needed, from the control operator or AMSAT.
notes.explanation: Receiving needs no licence and no permission: telemetry reports the satellite’s health and status to any listener, and no encryption key from anyone is required.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8B11, T8B01

notes.front: Which of the following is a way to determine whether your satellite uplink power into a linear transponder satellite is neither too low nor too high?
notes.back: Your signal strength on the downlink should be about the same as the beacon
notes.choices:
A) Check your signal strength report in the telemetry data
B) Listen for distortion on your downlink signal
C) Your signal strength on the downlink should be about the same as the beacon
D) Compare your signal to others on the downlink using an internet SDR receiver
notes.choicesExplained: A: telemetry reports the satellite's health, not your signal. B: distortion is not a reliable power gauge. D: comparing with other users does not give the satellite's reference level.
notes.explanation: The beacon is a steady reference on the downlink. If your signal comes back about as strong, you are loud enough without taking more than your share: too much uplink power blocks other users.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8B12, T8B02

notes.front: Which of the following methods is used to locate sources of noise interference or jamming?
notes.back: Radio direction finding
notes.choices:
A) Echolocation
B) Doppler radar
C) Radio direction finding
D) Phase locking
notes.choicesExplained: A: echolocation uses reflected sound, not radio. B: Doppler radar measures motion of reflecting objects. D: phase locking is a circuit technique.
notes.explanation: Radio direction finding locates a source by the direction of its signal.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8C01

notes.front: Which of these items would be useful for a hidden transmitter hunt?
notes.back: A directional antenna
notes.choices:
A) Calibrated SWR meter
B) A directional antenna
C) A directional wattmeter
D) All these choices are correct
notes.choicesExplained: A and C: SWR meters and directional wattmeters check your own feed line, not a signal's direction. D: since A and C are wrong, “all” is wrong.
notes.explanation: A directional antenna shows which way the hidden transmitter lies.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8C02

notes.front: What operating activity involves contacting as many stations as possible during a specified period?
notes.back: Contesting
notes.choices:
A) Simulated emergency exercises
B) Net operations
C) Hidden transmitter hunts
D) Contesting
notes.choicesExplained: A: simulated emergency exercises practise emergency traffic. B: nets are organised, directed exchanges. C: transmitter hunts use direction finding.
notes.explanation: Contest rules award points for contacts, so the aim is to work as many stations as possible in the set period.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8C03; Wikipedia, “Contesting”

notes.front: Which of the following is good practice when contacting another station in a contest?
notes.back: Sending only the minimum information needed for proper identification and the contest exchange
notes.choices:
A) Signing only the last two letters of your call if there are many other stations calling
B) Contacting the station twice to be sure that you are in his log
C) Sending only the minimum information needed for proper identification and the contest exchange
D) Adding “Please copy” before your exchange
notes.choicesExplained: A: you must give your full call sign. B: contacting a station twice wastes time and is not needed. D: “please copy” adds needless words.
notes.explanation: Short exchanges keep each contact quick when many stations are calling; your full call sign is still required for proper identification.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8C04; 47 CFR 97.119(a)

notes.front: What is a grid locator?
notes.back: A letter-number designator assigned to a geographic location
notes.choices:
A) A letter-number designator assigned to a geographic location
B) A letter-number designator assigned to an azimuth and elevation
C) An instrument for locating faults in power amplifiers
D) An instrument for radio direction finding
notes.choicesExplained: B: it gives a location, not a direction (azimuth and elevation). C and D: it is not an instrument.
notes.explanation: A short code such as KN28LH tells another station roughly where you are: it names an area on the map, not a direction to point an antenna.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8C05

notes.front: How is over the air access to Internet Radio Linking Project (IRLP) nodes accomplished?
notes.back: By using Dual-Tone Multi-Frequency (DTMF) signals
notes.choices:
A) By obtaining a password that is sent via voice to the node
B) By using Dual-Tone Multi-Frequency (DTMF) signals
C) By entering the proper internet password
D) By using Continuous Tone-Coded Squelch System (CTCSS) tone codes
notes.choicesExplained: A: no voice password is used. C: internet passwords are not how you access a node over the air. D: CTCSS tones do not give IRLP access.
notes.explanation: A radio’s keypad sends DTMF tones, and the IRLP node decodes them as the number of the node to connect to.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8C06; Wikipedia, “Internet Radio Linking Project”

notes.front: What is Voice Over Internet Protocol (VoIP)?
notes.back: A method of delivering voice communications over the internet using digital techniques
notes.choices:
A) A set of rules specifying how to identify your station when linked over the internet to another station
B) A technique employed to “spot” DX stations via the internet
C) A technique for measuring the modulation quality of a transmitter using remote sites monitored via the internet
D) A method of delivering voice communications over the internet using digital techniques
notes.choicesExplained: A: it is not an identification rule. B: spotting DX via the internet is a different service. C: it does not measure modulation quality.
notes.explanation: Linking systems such as IRLP and EchoLink use VoIP to carry voice between distant stations and repeaters over the internet.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8C07, T8C08, T8C09; Wikipedia, “EchoLink”

notes.front: What is the Internet Radio Linking Project (IRLP)?
notes.back: A technique to connect amateur radio systems, such as repeaters, via the internet
notes.choices:
A) A technique to connect amateur radio systems, such as repeaters, via the internet
B) A system for providing access to websites via amateur radio
C) A system for informing amateurs in real time of the frequency of active DX stations
D) A technique for measuring signal strength of an amateur transmitter via the internet
notes.choicesExplained: B: it does not give access to websites. C: it is not a DX spotting system. D: it does not measure signal strength.
notes.explanation: Each IRLP node joins a local radio to the internet, so a handheld user can talk through a distant repeater.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8C08; Wikipedia, “Internet Radio Linking Project”

notes.front: Which of the following protocols enables an amateur station to transmit through a repeater without using a radio to initiate the transmission?
notes.back: EchoLink
notes.choices:
A) IRLP
B) D-STAR
C) DMR
D) EchoLink
notes.choicesExplained: A: IRLP users always start from a radio. B and C: D-STAR and DMR are digital radio modes that need a radio.
notes.explanation: EchoLink lets a user transmit through a linked repeater from a computer, without a radio.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8C09

notes.front: What is required before using the EchoLink system?
notes.back: Register your call sign and provide proof of license
notes.choices:
A) Complete the required EchoLink training
B) Purchase a license to use the EchoLink software
C) Register your call sign and provide proof of license
D) At least a General Class license
notes.choicesExplained: A: there is no required EchoLink training. B: the software needs no purchased licence. D: the requirement is registration with proof of licence, not a General class licence.
notes.explanation: EchoLink requires you to register your call sign and prove you are licensed.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8C10

notes.front: What is an amateur radio station that connects other amateur stations to the internet?
notes.back: A gateway
notes.choices:
A) A gateway
B) A repeater
C) A digipeater
D) A beacon
notes.choicesExplained: B: a repeater retransmits on another frequency. C: a digipeater relays packets over the air. D: a beacon transmits for propagation observation.
notes.explanation: It bridges on-air users and an internet linking system; an IRLP node, which joins a radio to the internet, is one example.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8C11

notes.front: Which of the following is a digital communications mode?
notes.back: All these choices are correct
notes.choices:
A) Packet radio
B) IEEE 802.11
C) FT8
D) All these choices are correct
notes.choicesExplained: A, B and C are each only one digital mode; all are correct.
notes.explanation: Packet radio, IEEE 802.11 (Wi-Fi) and FT8 each send information as digital data rather than as analog voice, so all three are digital communications modes.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8D01

notes.front: What is FT8?
notes.back: A digital mode capable of low signal-to-noise operation
notes.choices:
A) A wideband FM voice mode
B) A digital mode capable of low signal-to-noise operation
C) An eight-channel multiplex mode for FM repeaters
D) A digital slow-scan TV mode with forward error correction and automatic color compensation
notes.choicesExplained: A: FT8 is a narrow data mode, not wideband FM voice. C: it is not a repeater multiplex. D: it is not a TV mode.
notes.explanation: FT8 sends short, slow messages with forward error correction, so it can be decoded even when the signal is weak and noisy.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8D02; Wikipedia, “FT8”

notes.front: What kind of data can be transmitted by APRS?
notes.back: All these choices are correct
notes.choices:
A) GPS position data
B) Text messages
C) Weather data
D) All these choices are correct
notes.choicesExplained: A, B and C are each only one kind of APRS data; all are correct.
notes.explanation: APRS carries any information of immediate local value, including GPS positions, text messages and weather data; positions are its best-known use, shown on a live map.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8D03; Wikipedia, “Automatic Packet Reporting System”

notes.front: What is meant by the term "NTSC?"
notes.back: An analog fast-scan color TV signal
notes.choices:
A) A digital transmission standard for encrypting data
B) A special mode for satellite uplink
C) An analog fast-scan color TV signal
D) A frame compression scheme for TV signals
notes.choicesExplained: A: it is analog, not a digital encryption standard. B: it is not a satellite uplink mode. D: it is not a compression scheme.
notes.explanation: NTSC is the analog colour TV signal that amateurs send as fast-scan TV, about 6 MHz wide; it is not digital, encrypted or a compression scheme.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8D04, T8A10

notes.front: Which of the following is an application of APRS?
notes.back: Providing real-time tactical digital communications in conjunction with a map showing the locations of stations
notes.choices:
A) Providing real-time tactical digital communications in conjunction with a map showing the locations of stations
B) Automatically showing the number of packets transmitted via PACTOR during a specific time interval
C) Providing voice over internet connection between repeaters
D) Providing information on the number of stations signed into a repeater
notes.choicesExplained: B: PACTOR is a separate radio data mode; counting its packets is not an application of APRS. C: linking repeaters over the internet is VoIP (IRLP, EchoLink). D: counting stations on a repeater is not APRS.
notes.explanation: APRS provides real-time tactical digital communications alongside a map of station locations.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8D05

notes.front: What does the abbreviation "PSK" mean?
notes.back: Phase Shift Keying
notes.choices:
A) Pulse Shift Keying
B) Phase Shift Keying
C) Packet Sampled Keying
D) Power Sampled Keying
notes.choicesExplained: A, C and D: “Pulse”, “Packet Sampled” and “Power Sampled” are invented expansions.
notes.explanation: PSK sends bits by shifting the phase of the carrier; in the simple two-state form, a one reverses the phase and a zero leaves it unchanged.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8D06; US Navy, NEETS Module 12 (NAVEDTRA 14184), Modulation, chapter 2, “Phase-Shift Keying”

notes.front: Which of the following describes DMR?
notes.back: A technique for time-multiplexing two digital voice signals on a single 12.5 kHz repeater channel
notes.choices:
A) A technique for time-multiplexing two digital voice signals on a single 12.5 kHz repeater channel
B) An automatic position tracking mode for FM mobiles communicating through repeaters
C) An automatic computer logging technique for hands-off logging when communicating while operating a vehicle
D) A digital technique for transmitting on two repeater inputs simultaneously for automatic error correction
notes.choicesExplained: B: automatic position tracking describes APRS. C: DMR is not a logging technique. D: DMR does not transmit on two repeater inputs.
notes.explanation: Two users take turns in rapid time slots, so one 12.5 kHz repeater channel carries two conversations at once.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8D07; Wikipedia, “Digital mobile radio”

notes.front: Which of the following is included in packet radio transmissions?
notes.back: All these choices are correct
notes.choices:
A) A checksum that permits error detection
B) A header that contains the call sign of the station to which the information is being sent
C) Automatic repeat request in case of error
D) All these choices are correct
notes.choicesExplained: A, B and C are each only one part of a packet transmission; all are correct.
notes.explanation: A packet transmission includes all three: a checksum that permits error detection, a header with the destination station’s call sign, and automatic repeat request if an error is found.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8D08

notes.front: What is CW?
notes.back: Another name for a Morse code transmission
notes.choices:
A) A type of electromagnetic propagation
B) A digital mode used primarily on 2-meter FM
C) Error correction for digital transmission using code words
D) Another name for a Morse code transmission
notes.choicesExplained: A: CW is not a propagation type. B: it is not a 2 m FM digital mode. C: it is not an error-correction scheme.
notes.explanation: CW sends Morse code by starting and stopping the carrier with a key.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8D09; US Army, FM 24-18, Tactical Single-Channel Radio Communications Techniques (1987), para 2-6 (“Radiotelegraphy”)

notes.front: Which of the following operating activities is supported by digital mode software in the WSJT-X software suite?
notes.back: All these choices are correct
notes.choices:
A) Earth-Moon-Earth
B) Weak signal propagation beacons
C) Meteor scatter
D) All these choices are correct
notes.choicesExplained: A, B and C are each only one of the supported activities; all are correct.
notes.explanation: WSJT-X supports all three: Earth-Moon-Earth (moonbounce), weak-signal propagation beacons and meteor scatter. Each involves very weak or very brief signals, which its modes are designed to decode.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8D10; Wikipedia, “WSJT (amateur radio software)”

notes.front: What is the role of ARQ in a transmission system?
notes.back: An error correction method in which the receiving station detects errors and sends a request for retransmission
notes.choices:
A) A special transmission format limited to video signals
B) A system used to encrypt command signals to an amateur radio satellite
C) An error correction method in which the receiving station detects errors and sends a request for retransmission
D) A method of compressing data using autonomous reiterative Q codes prior to final encoding
notes.choicesExplained: A: ARQ is not limited to video. B: it is not satellite command encryption. D: it is not a compression method.
notes.explanation: Like a listener saying “say again” whenever part of a message is garbled: the receiver checks each block of data and asks for any bad one to be sent again.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8D11

notes.front: Which of the following best describes an amateur radio mesh network?
notes.back: An amateur-radio data network using commercial Wi-Fi equipment with modified firmware
notes.choices:
A) An amateur-radio data network using commercial Wi-Fi equipment with modified firmware
B) A wide-bandwidth digital voice mode employing DMR protocols
C) An amateur-radio satellite communications network using modified commercial satellite TV hardware
D) An internet linking protocol allowing communication through repeaters around the world
notes.choicesExplained: B: it is a data network, not a DMR voice mode. C: it does not use satellite TV hardware. D: it is not an internet repeater-linking protocol like IRLP.
notes.explanation: Off-the-shelf Wi-Fi equipment is given modified firmware so that it runs as an amateur data network; Broadband-Hamnet is one such project.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8D12; Wikipedia, “Wireless mesh network”

notes.front: FM or SSB voice: which is narrower, and which receives only one signal at a time?
notes.back: SSB is narrower (about 3 kHz against 10–15 kHz); FM receives only one signal at a time.
notes.explanation: FM suits local repeater work; SSB's narrow signal suits weak-signal and long-distance work.
notes.contrast: SSB: about 3 kHz, weak-signal work. FM: 10–15 kHz, repeaters, one signal at a time.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8A07, T8A08, T8A09, T8A12

notes.front: IRLP or EchoLink: which can you use from a computer with no radio at all?
notes.back: EchoLink. IRLP users always talk from a radio and use DTMF tones to connect nodes.
notes.explanation: Because EchoLink reaches the air without a radio, it requires registration with proof of licence.
notes.contrast: IRLP: radio only, DTMF access. EchoLink: computer or radio, registration and proof of licence.
notes.source: Wikipedia, “EchoLink” and “Internet Radio Linking Project”; NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8C09, T8C10

notes.front: During a satellite pass, one signal fades in and out rhythmically and another drifts in frequency. Which effect is which?
notes.back: Rhythmic fading: spin fading, from the satellite's rotation. Frequency drift: Doppler shift, from relative motion.
notes.explanation: Spin fading changes strength; Doppler shift changes frequency. A tracking program predicts the Doppler shift.
notes.contrast: Spin fading: strength varies (rotation). Doppler: frequency varies (motion).
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8B07, T8B09, T8B03

notes.front: A beacon station on Earth and a satellite beacon: what does each transmit for?
notes.back: An Earth beacon lets others observe propagation; a satellite beacon sends the satellite's status information.
notes.explanation: Both are steady signals to listen for, but a satellite beacon carries telemetry about the spacecraft.
notes.contrast: Beacon station: propagation. Satellite beacon: health and status telemetry.
notes.source: 47 CFR 97.3(a)(9); NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8B05
